processing: Details for this grade are scarcely recorded. It was a leaf green tea of the Soviet Georgian range, graded above the numbered scale, and the same-named black grade was made from the top leaves of the bush with tips.
harvest_season: Little is documented for this grade. High grades in the Georgian system relied on fine upper leaves rather than machine-picked shoots.
appearance_dry: Few descriptions survive; a top-grade leaf green tea would be expected to be clean and even, with little stem.
appearance_liquor: Not specifically described; typical of good leaf green tea, a clear pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Not specifically described; as with other fine-plucked greens, small tender leaves.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting notes for this grade survive. Expect what is typical of a clean, high-grade green tea: fresh and lightly vegetal, with some grip.

brewing.notes: General advice for a leaf green tea, since no method specific to this grade is recorded.

vintage_note: A grade name from the Soviet Georgian nomenclature, not a vintage or seasonal product. Little is documented about its sale today; if a pack carries the name now, treat it as a trade name and judge it as you would any green tea, by a recent harvest date.
description:
Bouquet of Georgia was the top of the Soviet Georgian green tea range. Greens there carried numbers that rose with quality, and Bouquet stood outside and above that scale, together with Extra.

How exactly it was made is poorly recorded. The black tea grades called Bouquet and Extra were made from the top leaves of the bush and contained tips, and it is reasonable to read the green as a similar idea, though that is an inference rather than a recorded recipe.

No trustworthy tasting notes survive for this very tea, so anything specific should be taken with caution. As with other high-grade greens, use cooler water and a moderate steep.

If you find it today, ask who made it and when. The name carries Soviet-era prestige, and nothing guarantees that a modern packet follows the old grade.
history:
The grade is known from the Soviet period, when Georgia made several dozen trade grades of green tea, far more than of black. Accounts put Bouquet at the very top, though one Georgian account names No. 95 and Bouquet together as the best of the range.

The top Soviet Georgian greens are described as matching the best world standards of green tea. Little is documented on who created this grade or what became of it later.
